sections.title: Start here: the counterparty the corpus had not covered
ps: The DNV and Sargent & Lundy guides taught who decides whether a battery or solar plant is **{{bankability}}**-grade: the engineer who tests the design and reads the warranty. This guide teaches the seat beside that one at financial close — the **insurer**. A lender can make the developer buy an engineer's opinion; it cannot make a hailstorm, a fire or a bad irradiance year go away. Someone has to hold those risks for a fee, and the terms on which they hold them change how much debt the project can carry.

kWh Analytics is the worked example because it occupies an unusual position: it is a **{{managing general agent}}** — an underwriter with no balance sheet, writing policies on other companies' capital — that built its authority on data rather than on capital. Through it you meet the whole tower: the broker who brings the risk, the MGA who prices it, the carrier whose paper it is written on, the reinsurer behind the carrier, and the lender who reads the policy before it lends.

**What this guide deliberately leaves out:** the mechanics of the independent engineer's report (DNV guide), the owner's engineer and design review (Sargent & Lundy guide), and how a battery degrades (Fluence and Tesla guides). It assumes you know what a P50 forecast is and what a lender's debt-service coverage ratio does; both are defined again briefly where they first appear.

**One idea carries this guide.** Insurance converts a risk the lender cannot size into a fee the sponsor can budget. Every product here — the property policy, the revenue put, the parametric hedge — is a different way of making that conversion, and the difference between them is *what triggers the payment*.

sections.title: What insurance does in a project financing
ps: **A financing is a promise to repay debt out of a plant's cash flows.** The lender sizes the loan so that, in a bad-but-plausible year, the plant still earns enough to pay interest and principal with a margin to spare — the **{{DSCR}}**. The three things that break that promise are that the plant produces less than forecast, that the plant is damaged and stops earning, and that the counterparties who owe it money or warranties fail. The engineer's report addresses the first and the contracts the third. Insurance is how the second is handled, and — in the products this guide is about — it can be extended to the first.

**Property insurance** pays to repair or replace physical damage from named or all perils — hail, wind, fire, flood, earthquake, equipment breakdown — up to a limit per location, after a deductible. A lender requires it as a condition of the loan because a damaged plant that cannot be rebuilt cannot repay. Alongside it sits **{{business interruption}}** cover (the revenue lost while the plant is down) and, during construction, **{{delay-in-start-up}}** cover for the revenue lost if commissioning slips because of an insured event.

**Performance or revenue insurance** is a different animal. It pays not when something breaks but when the plant *earns less than expected* for reasons inside the policy's list — low sun, snow, equipment failure, design error. Because it turns a variable cash flow into a floored one, the lender can treat the floor as near-certain and size more debt against it. That is why this class of product is called a **{{credit enhancement}}**: it improves the credit quality of the borrower without changing the plant.

**Who buys and who pays.** The sponsor buys every policy and pays every premium; the lender is named as loss payee and its counsel and insurance adviser review the terms before close. The engineer, the lawyer and the insurance adviser therefore form a ring around the financing, each answering a question the credit committee will ask. An insurer's willingness to write a risk at a price is itself evidence to that committee: 'without it, insurance just won't participate,' as one broker put it about resilience measures in 2025.

**The number that ties it together.** kWh Analytics reports that its solar put lets sponsors raise 'approximately 10% more debt', and that its wind hedge generated 'approximately $6' and then '$7' of additional loan proceeds per dollar of premium. Read those as exchange rates between two things the sponsor can spend: premium today against cheaper capital for the life of the loan.

sections.title: How a managing general agent works, and why data is its licence
ps: **An MGA is an underwriter that rents a balance sheet.** A carrier grants it **{{delegated authority}}** — the right to quote, bind and often adjust claims on the carrier's paper, inside limits and rules the carrier sets: which asset classes, what share of an account, what maximum per location. The MGA does the specialist work the carrier does not want to staff — here, understanding hail stow angles, inverter fire rates and thermal-runaway analyses — and is paid a commission on the premium it writes, sometimes with a profit share if the book performs.

**Capacity is the product.** For an MGA, 'capacity' means the limit its carriers will let it put on one risk. kWh's history is a capacity ladder: a property programme launched in 2023 at USD 75 million of limits, 'USD 75 million per renewable energy project location' with full authority for solar and battery accounts and half of wind or construction accounts in 2024, 'up to $100 million per renewable energy project location' with 'minority asset classes' added in February 2026, plus a USD 20 million excess layer for storms since August 2025. Each rung was a carrier deciding the MGA's judgment could be trusted with more.

**Why the data is the licence.** A carrier delegates authority to an MGA that knows something it does not. kWh's claim is a database of '300,000+ zero-carbon projects and $150B in loss data' and a performance record 'assessing 30% of U.S. solar assets' — company figures, never audited. Whether or not the numbers are exact, the logic is what matters: the MGA's data lets it argue that a plant with 3.2 mm tempered glass and a verified 53-degree hail stow deserves a 72 percent lower catastrophe rate, and the carrier accepts the argument because the MGA has seen the losses.

**Surplus lines.** kWh's policies are '**{{surplus lines}}** products written by surplus lines insurers' — coverage placed with insurers not licensed in the state on an admitted basis, permitted for risks the admitted market will not write. The trade-off is stated on kWh's own site: 'surplus lines insurance carriers do not generally participate in state guaranty funds and insureds are therefore not protected by such funds'. A lender's counsel reads that line.

**What an MGA is not.** It is not a broker (the broker works for the insured; the MGA works for the carrier), not a carrier (it holds no risk), and not a reinsurer. When Beazley — a Lloyd's-managing specialty insurer — bought kWh in 2026, it bought the underwriting judgment and the data; the question the sale leaves open is whether it keeps renting Aspen's balance sheet or writes the risk on its own.

sections.title: Hail: the peril that prices utility-scale solar
ps: **Why hail and not fire.** kWh's loss database says 'hail accounts for 73% of total solar industry losses by damage amount' while being only 6 percent of incidents; GCube's competing study puts hail at 1.4 percent of claims and 54 percent of losses, and VDE Americas at 2 percent of claims. The shares disagree; the shape does not: hail is rare, and when it comes it destroys whole fields of glass at once. A **{{severe convective storm}}** is the meteorological label for the thunderstorm complexes that produce it, and those storms 'drove $60 billion in insured losses in 2025' across all lines.

**The physics an underwriter needs.** A hailstone's damage depends on its kinetic energy at impact, which rises with the cube of its diameter, and on the angle at which it strikes the glass. Two levers follow. **Glass**: thicker, fully tempered front glass survives more energy — kWh's model says '3.2mm/2mm glass/glass modules sustain up to 1.7x higher impact energies' than the standard 3.2 mm glass-polymer build, and pv magazine reports heat-strengthened glass 'generates claims $50,000/MW higher on average'. **Angle**: tilting the tracker to a steep **{{hail stow}}** so stones strike obliquely — a 75-degree stow 'would have reduced damage probability by 87%' against 60 degrees in a 2022 event, per kWh's Longroad case study.

**Why models are argued over.** Physics-based models, kWh reports, 'may be overestimating the benefit of hail stow by 48% for ~3in hail' — large stones at steep stow angles still break glass. The 2026 Solar Risk Assessment's headline is that 'hail-hardened modules plus robust stow' are both needed for 13 percent of the United States. For the underwriter this is not academic: the resilience credit is only worth giving if the mitigation actually moves the loss curve, so the MGA's data is also its argument with its own carrier.

**Telematics closes the loop.** In April 2026 kWh began taking live stow data from Nextpower trackers directly into its pricing model — the first time a renewables policy has been priced on an equipment feed rather than on a submission form. It is the same logic as a telematics box in a car: the insurer rewards behaviour it can see.

sections.title: The Solar Revenue Put: insuring the forecast
ps: **Start from the forecast.** An engineer models a solar plant's output as a distribution: the **{{P-50}}** is the level exceeded half the time, the P90 the level exceeded nine years in ten, the **{{P-99}}** almost always. Lenders size debt to the downside — typically the P90 or a one-year P99 — because they are paid the same whether the sun shines or not and lose if it does not. The gap between P50 and P90 is revenue the sponsor expects to earn but the lender will not count.

**What the put does.** kWh's Solar Revenue Put 'guarantees up to 95% of a solar project's expected energy output' for 10 to 25 years (30 under the SRP+ variant), against 'equipment failure, irradiance deficiency, weather, wildfire smoke, and other risks'. If output falls below the insured level, the policy pays the shortfall 'within 30 days to ensure timely debt service payments'. The lender can therefore size to 95 percent of P50 instead of to P90 — a shallower downside case, hence more debt: 'average debt sizing increases of 10%'.

**Why it is called a put.** In finance a put option gives its holder the right to sell at a fixed price; here the project 'sells' its shortfall to the insurer at the insured production level. The economics are those of an **{{insurance wrap}}** on the forecast rather than on the equipment: the insurer is betting that its data on 300,000 systems prices the forecast risk better than the lender's blanket haircut does. The premium is the sponsor's cost; the extra debt at a lower rate than equity is its gain.

**What lenders check before accepting it.** The carrier's rating ('investment grade financial ratings' — Swiss Re, then Everest); the tenor matching the loan (the 26-year Matrix Renewables policy was the first to cover a full amortisation); the perils list against the engineer's risk register; the exclusions; and the claims record, of which the only independent statement is a customer's in 2020: 'a reliable claims process'. Adoption figures — 'more than 40%' of lenders in 2019, 'over 50%' in 2020, '30+ major lenders' today — are the company's own.

**The pattern to notice.** Named put financings cluster in 2018–2023 and the company's own forward statements favour parametric structures. A credit enhancement is most valuable when lenders are conservative and capital is dear; in a soft market with cheap debt, the 10 percent uplift buys less.

sections.title: Two ways to pay: indemnity versus parametric
sections.intro: The property policy and the revenue put are indemnity products: they pay what you actually lost, after a claim is adjusted. The Wind Proxy Hedge is parametric: it pays a pre-agreed amount when a measured index — wind speed at the site — crosses a threshold, whether or not the project lost money. Each fits a different problem.

cards.meta: Pays the measured loss up to the limit, after deductible, once the claim is adjusted.
adv: **No basis risk** — if the plant is damaged or under-produces for a covered reason, the payment matches the loss.
**Familiar to lenders** — loss-payee clauses, adjusters and policy wordings are standard project-finance furniture.
**Covers the causes that matter** — equipment failure and design error, which no weather index captures.
dis: **Slow and contestable** — a claim must be documented, adjusted and sometimes disputed; the 30-day promise on the put is a company claim, not an industry norm.
**Moral hazard and exclusions** — the insurer needs O&M records, maintenance proof and exclusions to avoid paying for neglect.
**Capacity-hungry** — the carrier takes the full loss distribution, so limits and rates move with the catastrophe market.

cards.t: Parametric (Wind Proxy Hedge with Munich Re)
cards.meta: Pays a formula amount when measured wind speed falls below a threshold; the 'Indifference Structure' sets the threshold so the sponsor is indifferent between hedged and unhedged cases.
adv: **Fast and objective** — the trigger is a measurement, so payment does not wait on adjustment or argument.
**Prices cleanly** — a reinsurer or weather-derivatives desk can price a wind-speed distribution without underwriting the project's O&M.
**Improves the P99 directly** — 'adding investment-grade cash flow above the P99 wind speed', which is exactly the case the lender sizes to: '$7 of additional debt for every dollar of premium'.
dis: **Basis risk** — the wind can blow while a turbine is broken; the hedge pays for weather, not for the plant.
**Only for resource risk** — it cannot cover equipment failure, hail or fire.
**Bespoke** — two deals in two years; the structure is proprietary and each is negotiated with the arranger.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **The soft market erodes the thesis.** kWh's edge is pricing resilience. Its own 2026 Broker Council found 'property insurance rates for renewable energy assets have been reducing' and that 'the urgency to build more weather-resilient assets has somewhat diminished'. When capacity is abundant, a discount for stow angles is worth less — and a data-driven MGA competes with everyone else's cheap capacity.

**Sublimits and groupings.** Sponsors are 'pushing back against applying the same sublimits and restrictions to straight-line wind (derecho), tornadoes, and lightning' as to hail. A policy whose headline limit is USD 100 million can pay far less for the peril that actually strikes.
**Surplus lines.** No state guaranty fund stands behind a surplus-lines carrier. The promise is worth the carrier's rating and nothing more.

**Company claims that no one audits.** 'Over $50 billion of assets insured', '15 global reinsurers', '30% of U.S. solar assets', 'claims paid within 30 days' — all the company's own; the hail-share figure is contested by GCube and VDE; headcount is 39, 42 or 100–250 depending on the vendor. A reader should carry these as claims, exactly as the dossier does.

**Integration risk.** Beazley bought kWh in 2026 and Zurich is buying Beazley. The Aspen programme, the Swiss Re and Munich Re relationships and the kWh brand all sit inside a company that is being absorbed twice; nothing has been published since June 2026.
**Basis risk on the parametric side.** A wind hedge pays for weather, not for the plant. A broken turbine in a windy year is the sponsor's problem.

cards.q: What is a managing general agent, and what does it not hold?
cards.a: An underwriter that prices and binds policies under delegated authority from a carrier, paid by commission; it holds no insurance risk on its own balance sheet.

cards.q: Define delegated authority and give kWh's 2024 instance.
cards.a: The carrier's grant of power to an MGA to quote and bind on its paper inside limits — 'USD 75 million per location', full authority for solar and BESS, half for wind and construction (Aspen, 2024).

cards.q: Why is a revenue put called a credit enhancement?
cards.a: It floors the project's revenue so the lender can size debt to a shallower downside case — better credit without changing the plant.

cards.q: What does the Solar Revenue Put guarantee, for how long, and who paid the first one's claims?
cards.a: Up to 95 percent of expected (P50) output for 10–25 years (30 under SRP+); Swiss Re Corporate Solutions carried the early puts, Everest later.

cards.q: State the difference between an indemnity policy and a parametric hedge in one sentence each.
cards.a: Indemnity pays the measured loss after adjustment; parametric pays a pre-agreed amount when a measured index crosses a threshold, regardless of the actual loss.
The gap between what a parametric trigger pays and what the insured actually lost — the wind blew, but the turbine was broken.

cards.q: Why does hail dominate solar losses despite being rare?
cards.a: A single storm damages whole fields of glass at once; kinetic energy rises with the cube of stone diameter, so a few large-stone events carry most of the loss amount.

cards.q: Name the two levers a solar owner has against hail, and the trade-off in each.
cards.a: Thicker fully tempered glass (cost per module) and a steep hail stow (needs trackers that stow fast enough, and models overstate its benefit for very large stones).

cards.q: What is an excess layer and what is an attachment point?
cards.a: A layer of cover above the primary policy; the attachment point is the loss level at which it starts paying.

cards.q: What does 'surplus lines' mean for the insured?
cards.a: Cover from an insurer not admitted in the state — allowed for hard-to-place risks — with no state guaranty-fund protection if the carrier fails.

cards.q: What three things does a BESS property underwriter want in a submission?
cards.a: Chemistry and enclosure (outdoor LFP, spacing), UL 9540A and large-scale fire-test data showing no propagation, and a Hazard Mitigation Analysis with an Emergency Response Plan.

cards.q: Why does a one-year policy on a 35-year asset create tension?
cards.a: Capacity and price reset annually against a loan of 15–20 years; the lender's covenant assumes cover it cannot guarantee will renew.

cards.q: Who buys the policy and who benefits?
cards.a: The sponsor buys and pays; the lender is loss payee and reviews the wording before it lends.

cards.q: What did Beazley buy when it bought kWh Analytics?
cards.a: Underwriting judgment and a loss-and-performance database — not a balance sheet or a premium volume large enough to matter to a USD 6 billion insurer.

items.q: A lender sizes debt to the P90 case. A sponsor buys a put insuring 95 percent of P50 output for the loan's term. The most accurate description of what changed is:
c: The plant will now produce more energy
The lender can size to a shallower downside case, so more debt fits the same plant
The lender no longer needs an independent engineer
The premium is deducted from the P50 forecast
items.why: Nothing physical changed. The insurer now stands behind the gap between the P90 haircut and 95 percent of P50, so the lender's stress case is shallower and the debt sizing rises — kWh reports about 10 percent.

items.q: A wind project buys a parametric hedge that pays when measured wind speed falls below a threshold. In a windy year its gearbox fails for four months. The hedge:
c: Pays the lost revenue because the project earned less
Pays nothing, because the index did not trigger — that is basis risk
Pays half, as parametric hedges always split the loss
Voids because the project was not operating
items.why: Parametric products pay on the index, not the loss. Equipment failure is the indemnity products' domain — which is why kWh sells both.

items.q: An MGA's carrier withdraws its delegated authority at renewal. What happens to the policies already in force?
c: They are cancelled immediately
They continue to their expiry on the carrier's paper; the MGA can bind no new business on it
They transfer automatically to the MGA's own balance sheet
The insureds must refund the premium
items.why: The MGA never held the risk; the carrier did and still does until expiry. What the MGA loses is the ability to write — its capacity, which is its product.

items.q: The company reports hail as 73 percent of solar losses by amount and 6 percent of incidents; GCube reports 54 percent and 1.4 percent. The right reading for an underwriter is:
c: One of the studies is fraudulent
Both show the same shape — a rare peril carrying most of the loss amount — and the shares depend on whose book is measured
Hail is not a material peril
GCube's book must be in a different country
items.why: Loss shares are properties of a portfolio. Different books give different shares; the underwriting conclusion — price the tail, reward mitigation — is the same.

A parametric hedge instead
Cover only if the site adopts NFPA 855-2026 retroactively
items.why: The market's stated line: 'indoor BESS installations, particularly those using NMC chemistry, will face significantly higher scrutiny' while rates for current technology stayed 'stable at approximately 30-40 cents per US$100'.

Beazley bought underwriting capability and data, and whether kWh keeps renting Aspen's balance sheet is unresolved
The deal has a published price and completion date
Zurich blocked the deal
items.why: Beazley's CEO framed it as building 'transition underwriting capability'; no price, premium or completion release exists; Kaminsky's 'business as usual … with $100M per location capacity' describes March 2026, not the post-integration book.
